title: Costs that compound
desc: How small yearly fees grow into big gaps

cards.title: A small fee?
cards.situation: Two funds hold the same stocks. Fund A charges 0.1% a year, Fund B 1%. You put $10,000 in for 20 years. Roughly how big is the gap at the end?

options.feedback: The fee is taken from a growing pot, and the money it takes stops growing too. So the gap compounds.
Fees compound like returns do, just in the wrong direction.
1% a year looks tiny, but it’s taken every year from a growing pot. Over 20 years that adds up to thousands.

cards.work: Say 7% a year before fees. 0.1% fee: about $38,000. 1% fee: about $32,000. Gap: about $6,000.
cards.added: Feedback for C written for the Academy

cards.title: Costs compound
cards.text: Every year a fee takes a slice. Next year, that slice isn’t there to grow. Over decades, **small fees grow into big gaps**.

visual.title: $10,000 over 20 years
visual.label: $10,000 grows to about $38,000 with a 0.1% fee and about $32,000 with a 1% fee

blocks.tip: Round illustrative numbers, assuming 7% a year before fees. Real returns vary.

cards.title: The gap keeps growing
cards.text: Same $10,000, same 7% a year before fees. Only the fee is different.

visual.title: Value after fees
visual.label: Value after fees: 5 years $14.0k vs $13.4k, 10 years $19.5k vs $17.9k, 20 years $38.0k vs $32.1k

cards.added: The board’s gap rows are the tap-to-open notes on each year

cards.title: Too small to matter?
cards.myth: 1% a year is too small to matter.
cards.reality: Over 20 years, a 1% fee can take about a sixth of the final amount. Trading costs and spreads add more on top.
cards.rule: check the yearly fee before you buy any fund.
cards.added: Board P1-Ch09-L5 card 4: the fee rows (yearly fund fee: every year · trading fees and spreads: every trade)

cards.title: Price the fee
cards.q: You pay a 1% yearly fee on a $50,000 portfolio. How much is the fee this year?

options.feedback: $50 would be a 0.1% fee. 1% is ten times more.
1% of $50,000 is $500, and the fee grows as the pot grows.
$5,000 would be a 10% fee. 1% is a tenth of that.
$1,000 would be a 2% fee. Take 1% of $50,000.

cards.work: $50,000 × 1% = $500 this year, and more as the pot grows.

cards.title: Same index, two funds
cards.q: Two funds track the same index. What should you compare first?

options.feedback: Funds that track the same index earn almost the same before fees. The fee is the main real difference.
Funds that track the same index earn almost the same before fees, so the fee is the main real difference.
Popularity doesn’t change what the fund holds. The yearly fee is what changes your result.
A share’s price says nothing about cost. Same index, so compare the yearly fee.
